A · A room with the window open

A / 01 A room with the window open In the accounts collected by ethnographers in Russian villages from the middle of the nineteenth century onward, death is registered less as an event than as a series of adjustments to a house. Mirrors are covered. Water standing in the house is thrown out or covered. The body is washed and laid on a table under the icons, head toward them, and the household is rearranged around it. Across Eastern Slavic rites a window or door is opened for the soul to leave; the Russian-specific evidence read here for that is thinner. A stopped clock is often named, but no source read for this edition records it, so it is not asserted. These are the practices most often repeated in the literature, and they are the ones most often flattened into a single ‘Russian custom’. The sources do not support that flattening. They record variants; they record disagreement between villages a day’s walk apart; and they record the informant’s own uncertainty about why a thing was done.
A · The soul as breath, and as a guest

A / 02 The soul as breath, and as a guest Russian folk belief, as described by Linda Ivanits and by D. K. Zelenin before her, treats the soul (dusha) as a substance closely bound to breath and to the body’s warmth, and simultaneously as a person-like visitor who must be housed, fed and escorted. These are not two beliefs held by different people; they are two grammars used in the same account. The consequence is a threshold that is both physical and social. The dead remain members of the household for a defined period, are addressed in the second person, and are given food and a place at the table. The border is maintained by small prohibitions rather than by a wall.
A · Premonitions, and the problem of the motif

A / 03 Premonitions, and the problem of the motif Recorded 19th–early 20th c. Folklore motif; prevalence not established Folk narrative A dog howling at night, a bird striking the window, a beam groaning in the wall, a double shadow: the folkloric record is full of signs read retrospectively as announcements of a death. Published collections treat them as motifs, not as statistics. No source used here establishes how widely any single sign was believed, and retrospective reading makes such reports structurally unreliable.
A · Three claims we did not confirm

Uncertainty register Three claims we did not confirm That the mirror was covered to prevent the soul from being trapped. The practice is widely reported; the explanation is supplied by later writers and varies. That a body was always carried out feet first. Reported in some regional descriptions; we did not verify its distribution or age. That the forty-day period is pre-Christian in origin. The scheme is documented in Orthodox liturgical handbooks; the claim that it continues an older pagan calendar is an interpretation, and a contested one.

B / 01 Washing The body is washed (obmyvanie) before it is dressed. The task is generally given to people from outside the immediate family — commonly older women, sometimes women who have performed it before — and the work is understood as a service that must be paid for, in soap, towels or money. The washing is practical and it is also a boundary: the living handle the dead at arm’s length and then wash themselves. The water used is not poured out where the household draws water. In accounts from different provinces it is carried away, poured at a threshold, or given to the ground. The variation is the point: the sources describe a prohibition around disposal, not one fixed method.
B · Clothing kept for the occasion

B / 02 Clothing kept for the occasion Dress for the dead was, in many households, prepared during life and stored: a bundle known in different places as smertnoe — ‘the death clothes’. It might include linen, a shirt or dress, stockings, sometimes a shroud. To have it ready was considered a form of decency, and its absence a small scandal. Once dressed, the body was placed in the coffin and the coffin placed so that the dead faced the icons. The position is an argument in wood and cloth: the dead is oriented toward the images of salvation, not toward the household. The living keep the door; the dead keep the corner.

B / 03 The coffin as furniture Planks; surviving dugout examples in northern descriptions 19th–20th c. Container, bed, and public stage The coffin (grob) appears in the ethnography with an emphasis on plainness, but also with ornament: a lid, a shawl, a cross on the lid. In some northern descriptions coffins were hollowed from a single trunk; by the late imperial period the sawn plank coffin was standard and increasingly a purchased object rather than a made one. Between the two lies a commercial history that the ritual sources rarely discuss: the coffin is where the funeral economy becomes visible, first as carpentry, later as an industry.

B · Why the body is a difficult archive

Method Why the body is a difficult archive The body leaves no object. What survives is the description of the objects that surrounded it, written down later, often by outsiders. Ethnographers of the nineteenth century tended to record what they judged to be old. The date of a practice is therefore often the date of its recording, not of its origin.
C · The shape of the forty days

C / 01 The shape of the forty days The commemoration of the dead on the third, ninth and fortieth day after death is set out in Orthodox liturgical handbooks, and the reasons given there are theological rather than calendrical. In the nineteenth-century handbook Novaia Skrizhal’, the third day is tied to the Resurrection, the ninth to the nine ranks of angels, and the fortieth to the Ascension, which took place on the fortieth day. The same handbook is explicit that the prayers are for the forgiveness of sins and the placing of the soul ‘with the saints’. The popular explanations that accompany the scheme — that the soul visits the house for three days, that it is examined on the ninth, that it finally departs on the fortieth — belong to a different register. They are widespread, they are recorded, and they are not the doctrine.

C / 02 Against the survival story Nineteenth- and early twentieth-century scholarship often read Russian funerary practice as a survival of pre-Christian religion, with the Church imposed on top. Later work on ritual has been more cautious. A. K. Baiburin’s study of ritual in traditional culture treats ritual as a system of signs with its own internal logic rather than as a fossil of an earlier belief; the question of what a rite ‘originally meant’ is usually unanswerable from the evidence that survives. This atlas therefore marks origin claims as interpretations. The forty-day cycle is documented as Christian. Whether some households also understood it as an older calendar is a question the sources used here cannot settle.

C / 03 Who does the work Female mourners, readers, priest, household 19th–20th c. Ethnographic descriptions; parish sources The ritual has an economy of roles. The priest serves; a reader may read the psalter; women lament; neighbours cook and carry. The laments (see plate G) are performed by women who are often, but not always, kin, and their performance is judged — for voice, for fullness, for the ability to make the room weep. The distribution of labour is itself historical. In the Soviet period the priest’s role contracted and the household’s expanded; after 1991 it contracted back again in some places and not in others.

A date given in a source may not correspond to the date a family used. Memorial days also differ by region and by parish practice. The scheme above is a frame, not a census.

D / 01 The hot dinner On the day of burial the household feeds everyone who came. In the ethnography this meal has a name in each region — ‘hot dinner’, ‘hot table’ — and a fixed grammar: a first course that is eaten before anything else, a place kept for the dead, a portion set aside, food carried to the grave. The meal is commemoration, and it is also accounting: those who washed, dug, carried, read and cooked are fed, and the household’s obligation is discharged in food. To refuse to sit at the table is to refuse the account.

D · Kutia, and the ambiguity of grain

D / 02 Kutia, and the ambiguity of grain Kutya is boiled grain sweetened with honey, and in its church form — kolivo — it is brought to the memorial service and blessed. The grain is read as a figure of resurrection: it is buried, it does not remain buried. The reading is old and it is also obvious enough to have been made many times independently. What the sources do not settle is the relationship between the church dish and the household dish. In some accounts they are the same object under two names; in others the household kutya is a separate, richer preparation with raisins or nuts. The atlas keeps both, and keeps the question open.
D · Why a Ukrainian photograph is here

Outside Russia Why a Ukrainian photograph is here The atlas treats ‘Russian’ as a language, a state tradition and a set of institutions, not as a synonym for East Slavic. Where a photograph documents a Ukrainian or Belarusian practice, it is labelled as such. The meal at the grave is widely attested across the region, which makes it exactly the kind of practice that gets mislabelled as ‘Russian’ by default.

E / 01 Zelenin’s ‘pledged’ dead In 1916 D. K. Zelenin published a study of those who die an unnatural death — by suicide, accident, murder, drowning, or before their time — and of the rusalki. His term for them, zalozhnye pokoiniki, is usually translated as ‘pledged’ or ‘unclean’ dead: those whose death was not completed within the order of things. Zelenin argued that such dead were buried apart, outside the cemetery or at its edge, in ravines, fields or at crossroads, and that they were believed to remain active — to walk, to appear, to harm. The book is a work of synthesis and it is also a work of its time, assembled from scattered reports into a system that no single informant would have recognised.

E / 02 The dispute Later scholarship has treated Zelenin’s category with caution. The reports he gathered come from different provinces, different decades and different genres — legend, memorate, custom, ecclesiastical prohibition — and the boundary between ‘unclean’ and ‘clean’ death was drawn differently from place to place. Whether the rusalka is a development of the unclean dead, as Zelenin proposed, remains an interpretation rather than a finding. The atlas therefore presents zalozhnye as a scholarly construction built on real reports, not as a folk taxonomy that everyone shared. The reports are evidence. The category is an argument.
E · Case notes, without the case

E / 03 Case notes, without the case Ethnographic report, legend, memorate 19th–early 20th c. No individual narrative is quoted here The reports share a structure: a death that violates expectation, a burial that violates place, and a subsequent sighting or disturbance. The disturbance is usually resolved by a ritual action — moving the body, reading a prayer, driving a stake, calling the priest — and the resolution tells us more about the living than about the dead. No narrative is reproduced verbatim in this atlas. The genre is highly variable, the published texts are often retold rather than transcribed, and a single vivid quotation would misrepresent the record as more uniform than it is.
E · What the category was for

E / 04 What the category was for The unclean dead mark the limits of the community’s obligation. They are the people for whom the full ritual was not, or could not be, performed — and the fear they provoke is the fear of an obligation left unpaid. In this reading the revenant is less a monster than an unpaid debt with a voice. That reading is the atlas’s interpretation, offered as such. It does not require the dead to be real; it requires the living to have accounts.

Caution No vampires here Russian and Ukrainian records do contain stories of the dead who rise and feed, and the word upyr’ is attested. It is not the same figure as the nineteenth-century literary vampire, and it should not be used to give this material a familiar costume. The atlas avoids the vocabulary of horror. ‘Returning’ is a social event in these sources, not a genre.
A bad death is the one that leaves something owing, not the one that hurts most. Editorial note

F / 01 The decree of 1723 By a decree of Peter I dated 10 October 1723, burials inside towns were restricted — ‘except for notable persons’ — because the churchyards at churches and monasteries had become overcrowded. The same decree ordered the levelling of raised tombs and the replacement of relief images on shrines with painted ones. The measure did not last. After Peter’s death in 1725, churchyard burial resumed, and it took the catastrophe of 1771 to produce a durable change. In that year plague in Moscow killed in the tens of thousands, and the new cemetery at Vagankovo was founded to receive them; the first burials there were unnamed Muscovites.
F · The cemetery as a municipal object

F / 02 The cemetery as a municipal object From the late eighteenth century the cemetery moved out of the parish and into the city’s administration: walls, gates, a plan, a register, a fee. The dead acquired an address. This is the moment at which the Russian cemetery becomes legible as an institution — and the moment at which the difference between a churchyard and a necropolis becomes visible. By the nineteenth century the cemetery was also a place of class. The monastery necropolis, the merchant plot, the communal trench and the unconsecrated ground outside the wall were all parts of one landscape, and they were not equally maintained.
F · The roof over the cross

F / 03 The roof over the cross The golubets — a cross sheltered by a small gabled roof, sometimes enclosed as a little house — is one of the most distinctive grave forms recorded in the Russian North and in old cemeteries elsewhere. The roof protects the wood; it also makes the cross into a building, and the grave into a dwelling. The atlas does not map its distribution. Published claims about the ‘northern’ range of the form rest on surveys this project has not consulted, and a photograph of one example is not a distribution.
F · Novodevichy: the necropolis as biography

F / 04 Novodevichy: the necropolis as biography Novodevichy Cemetery in Moscow became, in the Soviet period, the place where the state buried its recognised dead: writers, scientists, generals, cosmonauts. The graves are biographical objects. The stonecutter’s lettering, the portrait, the open book, the ship, the aircraft — each monument is a curriculum vitae in granite. Two examples recorded in the photographs used by this atlas: the grave of Ilya Ilf, and a double monument for the writer A. N. Stepanov and his wife, designed — according to the photographer’s description — as two ships on a dark sea. The atlas repeats that description as a description, not as a documented intention of the family.

Unverified Portraits on stone Photographic portraits set into headstones are a familiar feature of late-Soviet and post-Soviet cemeteries. The atlas has not found a scholarly source for their chronology and does not date them here. The same caution applies to the enamel photograph, the plastic wreath and the metal fence: visible everywhere, documented in the sources used here almost nowhere.

G / 01 Barsov’s north Between 1872 and 1886 E. V. Barsov published Prichitaniia Severnogo kraia — ‘Laments of the Northern Land’ — in three volumes. The collection is the foundational document of Russian lament studies: texts recorded in the Olonets region, with the circumstances of performance, the performers and their repertoires. Laments are not spontaneous weeping set to words; they are composed in performance from a stock of formulas, by performers who know the genre and are judged by it. Barsov’s volumes make this visible: the same formulas recur across different deaths, recombined.
G · The score of a lament

G / 02 The score of a lament Funeral lament (prichitanie) Olonets province, 1870s Formulaic, performed, address in the second person An analytical reconstruction of the genre’s movement, after Barsov’s volumes: an address to the dead; a question about the journey; a complaint against the household’s new order; self-reproach by the survivor; a description of the grave; a farewell that refuses to be final. The order is not fixed, and the performer may return to any station. This is a structural description, not a text. The atlas does not print a lament here because a responsible quotation requires collation against a printed source and a translation the reader can check, and this edition has done neither.

G / 03 The second person Russian funerary language keeps the dead in the second person and in the present tense for as long as the ritual lasts. The dead is addressed by kin term — ‘my child’, ‘my master’, ‘my sister’ — and asked questions that presume an answer. The euphemisms that surround death in ordinary speech (ushel — ‘he has gone’; ne stalo — ‘he is no more’) are suspended in the lament, where the dead is named and spoken to directly. Death is not denied here. The border is held by hand: the dead person counts as present for exactly as long as the ritual lasts, and is then let go.

H / 01 What the Church says Orthodox teaching holds that the dead are judged and that the living may pray for them. The funeral rites ask for the forgiveness of sins and for a place ‘with the saints’; memorial services repeat the request at intervals. The fortieth day is the last of the appointed commemorations; the annual commemoration continues after it. The Church’s language is deliberately restrained about the intermediate state. Where popular literature supplies a detailed itinerary — where the soul goes on which day, what it sees — the atlas marks that as devotional or folk elaboration, not as doctrine.

H / 02 Reading the icon The Last Judgment icon is a diagram as much as a painting. Christ appears in glory; the scales weigh souls; the righteous move toward the heavenly city; the damned descend into a river of fire; the punishments are arranged in small compartments, each with its own inscription and its own social type — the miser, the adulterer, the usurer, the drunkard. The Volga icon used here belongs to the eighteenth century and to the urban artisan milieu: it borrows heavily from printed engravings, including their page-like blocks of text. This is no remote medieval image but a picture grown out of print, made for people used to reading with their eyes.

H · Theology is not a mood

Caution Theology is not a mood The icon’s punishments are evidence of a moral taxonomy, so the atlas does not use them as atmosphere or decoration. Where a popular belief contradicts or exceeds the Church’s formulation, the atlas says so rather than harmonising them.

I / 01 1771: the pit The Moscow plague of 1771 killed in the tens of thousands. The dead were buried outside the city, and the new cemetery at Vagankovo received, first of all, unnamed people. The historical account of the cemetery begins with a number it cannot disaggregate. Mass death produces this kind of record: a pit, a total, a name for the place, no names for the people. The atlas does not illustrate the pit. It prints the fact of it.

I / 02 The unknown soldier The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Kremlin wall was opened on 8 May 1967. The monument was designed by the architects Dmitrii Burdin, Vladimir Klimov and Iurii Rabaev, with the sculptor Nikolai Tomskii; the remains had been brought from a mass grave outside Moscow. The eternal flame was lit at the opening and has been maintained since. The unknown soldier is a very specific solution to a problem of scale: it converts an unmanageable number into a single body that can be visited. What it gains in ritual focus it loses in information. The state’s memory is built on that trade.

I / 03 Unburied Alexander Etkind’s Warped Mourning argues that Soviet culture was shaped by deaths that were not buried properly — the executed, the disappeared, the dead in unmarked ground — and that literature and memory-work in Russia have repeatedly returned to them as the ‘undead’. The argument is a cultural history, not a survey of graves, and the atlas presents it as an interpretation. Catherine Merridale’s Night of Stone makes a related point from the side of the living: the twentieth century in Russia produced so much death that mourning itself became a skill that had to be managed, suppressed, or performed in private. Both books are used here for their arguments, not as inventories of fact.
I · Why there are no bodies here

Restraint Why there are no bodies here This plate uses no photographs of corpses, no photographs of starving people, no images of the blockade dead. The atlas treats these as deaths, not as imagery. The monuments are shown because they are what the state built, and because their surfaces are evidence of how memory was organised.

J / 01 Perov, 1865 Vasily Perov’s Seeing Off the Dead (Provody pokoinika, 1865; oil on canvas, 45.3 × 57 cm; Tretyakov Gallery, inv. 5248) is small, and it is composed around a box. A peasant family rides a sled through snow; the coffin is tied behind them; a dog runs alongside. The widow sits with her back to us; the children face us. What the picture shows is a delivery. The body is hauled across a landscape that takes no notice: huge sky, flat snow, a few bare trees. Grief here behaves like weather. The Tretyakov Gallery’s own catalogue note connects the painting to Nekrasov’s poem Frost, Red Nose (1862–63), which describes a peasant family that has lost its breadwinner. The comparison was made by contemporaries and has been repeated by art historians; it is a documented reception, not a proof of intention.
J · The deathbed as a room

J / 02 The deathbed as a room Russian prose of the nineteenth century returns again and again to the deathbed as a place where a life is suddenly legible. Tolstoy’s The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886) is built as a corridor: the dying man moves through pain, denial and an unexpected opening at the end. Chekhov’s early story The Death of a Clerk (1883) makes the same subject ridiculous: a man dies of embarrassment. Bunin’s The Gentleman from San Francisco (1915) puts a wealthy man’s death in a hotel and refuses to grant it dignity. Three stories, three verdicts, no common school. Each uses a death to test the social order, and each gets a different result.
J · The square that was a gravestone

J / 03 The square that was a gravestone Kazimir Malevich died in 1935 and was buried, according to the account in the Moscow press, near Nemchinovka outside Moscow, under a lone oak. A white cube with a black square was placed on the grave. The oak was later cut down, the grave was lost, and the cube disappeared. What survives is a photograph and a painting. The black square began as an argument about painting, turned into a grave marker, and then vanished. Nowhere else in this atlas does an artwork and a missing grave coincide so exactly.

K · A crematorium in a church

K / 01 A crematorium in a church In 1925 the Moscow Soviet decided to build a crematorium and chose, as its site, the church of St Seraphim of Sarov and St Anna of Kashin at the Donskoy Monastery. The furnace was made by a German firm; the first cremation took place on 12 January 1927, and the official opening was held on 6 October 1927, without ceremony, according to the Moscow press account. A church built for burying bodies and praying for the dead became a furnace for making them disappear. The state did not have to design a new building; it confiscated one.

K / 02 The civil funeral The Soviet funeral was a ceremony without a priest: a hall, a portrait, an orchestra, a speech, a red coffin, medals carried on cushions, a grave in a designated section. The ritual was designed to be legible, repeatable and secular, and it was administered by the same municipal apparatus that handled housing and sanitation. Grief did not go away. It got a script and a timetable. Merridale’s account of the twentieth century is largely about what happened when the script and the experience did not match — and about the private, domestic mourning that continued alongside the public one.

K / 03 After 1991 The post-Soviet funeral is a market. Private funeral homes, municipal cemeteries with fee schedules, monument workshops, wreath sellers and, more recently, online memorial pages form an industry that the Soviet system had tried to keep inside the state. Orthodox practice returned in parallel — sometimes inside the same funeral, with the priest arriving after the orchestra. The atlas has not found a reliable scholarly account of this transition in the sources used here. This section is therefore marked as an editorial sketch, and the digital memorial is marked as an open question rather than described as a fact.

Open question The digital grave Online memorial pages, QR codes on headstones and social-media profiles of the dead are visible in contemporary Russia, but the atlas has not verified their scale, chronology or legal status. They are recorded here as a research task, not as a finding.

The dead are moved, or not moved; the stones are reused as paving or foundation; the register is lost. What remains is a place-name and a photograph taken before. This plate collects the forms of absence the atlas has actually encountered: a grave whose monument has disappeared, a cemetery photographed but not surveyed, a photograph whose subject is unidentified, a practice described only in a footnote.

M · A house that has been broken

M / 01 A house that has been broken Maria Andryunina’s survey of Ukrainian, Belarusian, western Russian and Polish funeral rites reports that at a death doors and windows were opened and holes made in the roof or ceiling, so that death could come in and the soul go out. By her account the house was then treated as broken. Its sacred boundaries were annulled, and an unsettled soul could haunt it, which made it dangerous for the living. The corpus matters. The rites in that article come from the western and southern fringes of the Eastern Slavic world and from Poland, and the plate does not offer them as a single Russian custom. The same article reports the reverse for new buildings: a newly built house counted as incomplete until the first death within it.

M / 02 The window Jelena Lewkijewskaja’s study of the window in the traditional culture of the Eastern Slavs treats it as a ritual entrance and exit between this world and the other. In funeral rites and in legends about death it is the route by which the souls of the dead, and mythological figures, enter and leave the house. Throwing something out of a window is a way of disposing of a dangerous or impure thing. In the same tradition a house without windows is the dwelling of someone alien, a being from another world. Put beside the open windows of the deathbed, this gives a dwelling whose openings are working parts of the rite. The study is five pages long and generalises across all the Eastern Slavs, and only its abstract was available to the atlas. It frames the question; it does not describe any one village.
M · The coffin as a house

M / 03 The coffin as a house Anna Plotnikova’s essay on the earthly places of death starts from the Slavic idea of death as a passage to another world, where the dead acquire a home. The coffin, the grave and the graveyard are read as that home’s earthly forms. A coffin is sometimes built like a house, with window openings, and its inside can copy a living home: an icon corner, bedding, everyday things. Funeral laments call it a cold, dark house without windows, and some words for ‘coffin’ derive from the word for ‘house’. On the same reading the dead remain tied to the home they left, and funeral customs work at separating them from it, by changing the route out of the house or by removing the dead person’s belongings. The essay covers Slavic traditions broadly. Which of these details are recorded for Russian regions has not yet been traced, and the bibliographic record for the essay is incomplete (see the source note).

N / 01 Outside the fence Dmitry Zelenin’s 1916 essays on those who died an ‘unnatural’ death collect local reports that such people were not always laid in the churchyard. Two are used here. At Orkino, in Saratov uezd, sudden deaths, drunkards, the drowned and suicides were buried far from the village, in the forest, in a ravine between two steep hills. In Silinskaya volost, Simbirsk guberniya, a ‘deaf forest ravine’ was held to be the proper grave for someone who had drunk himself to death, and burial in the cemetery was said to bring drought and crop failure. Both are reports in someone else’s book, read here through excerpts. The Orkino report concerns half-Russified Mordvins. Zelenin’s own conclusions about two classes of the dead have been revised since, and the plate takes from him only what local people were reported to do and to fear.
N · The forest on the road

N / 02 The forest on the road A 2025 comparative study of forest spirits by Mare Kõiva, Elena Boganeva and Ilya Butov remarks that in many rural cultures the forest is a place of hostile forces, or even of hell, and that the road to the realm of the dead is thought to run through it. The authors take that remark from an earlier author, Ivanov (1992), and present it as a common belief, not as their own finding. The article’s sources are archives in Estonia and Belarus, with a small Russian-language sample from Estonia. It supports a widespread idea; it does not show how that idea was held in any Russian village.
N · A hut at the treeline

N / 03 A hut at the treeline Enrique Santos Marinas, reading the folktales Afanasyev published between 1855 and 1863, argues that the hut of Baba-Yaga stands at the forest edge or in a clearing because that position marks it as a threshold between two realms. On his reading the hut is a gateway to the Other World and its owner guards the passage. This is a reading of narrative. A tale tells us what a teller expected an audience to recognise, which is not the same as what anyone did with a body. The plate keeps the hut as an image and does not use it as a record of belief.

O / 01 A landscape in between Olga Lavrenova’s essay reads swamps in the mythopoetic picture of the peoples of Russia as a border landscape. A swamp joins water and land without being either, and in many of her examples it is also a place where souls go and where the living are in danger. Swamp spirits drag people down or lure them into the mire, and the kikimora of some accounts is a girl who drowned in a swamp. The essay is a humanities argument built on secondary collections and has no stated way of choosing its examples. It ranges across Slavic, Finno-Ugric, Tungus, Turkic and other peoples, so a single detail cannot be assumed to be Russian. It tells us what a swamp can mean in these traditions. It does not tell us what any family did when someone drowned.

O / 02 The drowned at Semik The Great Russian Encyclopedia’s online entry on Semik, the Thursday of the seventh week after Easter, describes it as a time to remember people who died without repentance or a funeral: the drowned, the hanged, victims of violence and the unidentified. In Vyatka the day was given to the drowned, and cemetery feasts there turned boisterous. In Smolensk province people avoided washing, rinsing or any work with water on that day so that no one in the family would drown. Wreaths and birches were thrown into rivers, and in some readings whether a wreath floated or sank signalled marriage or death. The entry is anonymous and undated, and it names its regions without quoting the original records. The plate takes them as reports to be checked, not as a finished survey.

O / 03 Pits for the unclaimed The same entry says that unidentified and unclaimed bodies were once placed in open communal pits, skudelnitsy, and buried together at Semik. Commemoration took place at cemeteries and at the sites of these ‘poor houses’. It adds that Catherine II banned burial in them in 1771. That is a record of an institution, a place and a date. It is useful here because it shows the calendar custom attached to a physical arrangement for the dead who had no family to bury them. It says nothing about rivers.

P · Parting at the last crossroads

P / 01 Parting at the last crossroads N. A. Krinichnaya’s 1997 article on the crossroads, the Russian rosstan, records that it was the usual place to see travellers off and to wait for relatives returning after a long absence. The custom of parting at the village edge, at the nearest crossroads, she says, survived into her own time. Her material is mainly from the Russian North: Karelia, the Onega region, Vologda and Kostroma. The article’s subject is fate, and parting is a side topic that it handles briefly. It gives no figures for how common the custom was.
P · A crossing as a burial ground

P / 02 A crossing as a burial ground Krinichnaya traces burial at crossroads to ancestor cults. In her reading a clan ancestor’s ashes were set on a pillar where roads met, a practice she links to a passage in the Primary Chronicle. She describes the later burial of people who died ‘unnaturally’, such as suicides, the drowned and unbaptised infants, at crossroads as a degenerate form of that older rite. This is a reconstruction. It rests on fragmentary and often nineteenth-century records and on the idea of survivals, and the author’s own framing makes much of it hypothetical. The plate offers it as one scholar’s argument. It does not establish that any particular dead person was buried at any particular crossing.

P / 03 The roadside today M. G. Matlin’s geographical study recorded every roadside memorial sign on sections of three federal highways in the Middle Volga, photographing each, noting its coordinates and asking road workers and residents about it. He drove the routes repeatedly between 2013 and 2021 and documented 299 signs, whose dates of death run from 1965 to 2019. He sorts them into two families. One imitates the cemetery with crosses, steles, obelisks, fenced plots and wreaths. The other does not, and uses flowerpots, gazebos, decorated trees and car parts. The boundary between them is loose. Placement differs by region: in Mordovia most signs stand on slopes, in Tatarstan in the roadside strip and in Chuvashia in or near woodland. He argues this differs from the European and North American habit of placing memorials right at the road edge.

R · A cemetery cut into a ravine

R / 01 A cemetery cut into a ravine The Pskov-Caves Monastery at Pechory, near the Estonian border, is built over a system of burial caves. A pilgrim reference describes the near caves as the monastery cemetery, used at first only to bury monks. A 2023 newspaper account counts seven accessible underground ‘streets’ with a combined length of more than 200 metres. The figure repeated everywhere is about ten thousand burials. The pilgrim reference gives it as a total and the newspaper as a report; neither names a register. The plate carries the number as a reported size, not as a count.

R / 02 Looking behind the walls In 2023 a team of physicists, led according to the newspaper by N. G. Polukhina, laid nuclear-emulsion detectors in the caves to record atmospheric muons, which pass through rock and leave tracks where the rock is thinner or hollow. The method is non-destructive. A paper in the Bulletin of the Lebedev Physics Institute reports it for two objects in the cave complex. The newspaper account gives the results as reported by the team: a hidden passage about 12 m long behind a walled crypt, the continuation of Trinity Street into the hill beyond a barrier, and an unidentified cavity of roughly 3 × 6 × 3 m between two streets. These dimensions are the team’s estimates as quoted, not measurements anyone has opened up and checked. The same account says it is hard to know who dug the spaces, when and why. The question of what lies behind the walls is open, and the plate leaves it open.

R / 03 The tunnel to Izborsk Both a 2024 business-newspaper article and the 2023 Rosatom feature repeat the legend that the caves run underground from Pechory to Izborsk. The first puts the distance at about 20 km, the second at about 15 km. The Rosatom feature calls the tunnel legends unverified folklore and attributes them to the monastery’s abbot. The legend is kept here because it is told, not because it is true. The survey described above looked at two dead ends; it does not bear on a tunnel of that length.

S · A householder who may have been a relative

S / 01 A householder who may have been a relative Ethnographic work on Russian belief describes the domovoy as the spirit of a house and its people. O. K. Ansimova and O. V. Golubkova, drawing on an earlier study by N. A. Krinichnaya, call him a generic ancestor: the soul of an ancestor that became the soul of the house and the family. Some of their rural informants still held that view. The link to the dead runs through events. The same article says the domovoy may be the restless soul of a dead relative, that before a death he may knock or rattle dishes, and that after one he may disturb the house for a period such as forty days. In villages, food was set out for him at commemorations of dead parents.

S / 02 One village, 2019 M. A. Granova recorded beliefs about the domovoy in Severny Kommunar, in the Sivinsky district of Perm Krai, in June 2019 and compared them with older university-archive material from other districts. Speakers call him domovoy or dedushka-domovoy, ‘grandfather’. She reads such names as possibly pointing to a family ancestor or a dead elder who became the spirit of the house, and the diminutives as a way of appeasing him without naming him. He is described as a small hairy old man or as an animal, most often a cat or a weasel, and some say only children under five, cats and dogs can see him. Sweets are left for him; tables are not left empty overnight; a fixed formula is spoken to take him to a new house. Some speakers also describe a second, harmful female spirit in the cellar, which Granova says is not recorded elsewhere in the Perm archives she used. She finds the beliefs much reduced: the spirit has become a figure for frightening children or is merged with the unclean force in general, and the name Kuzka probably comes from a cartoon. She gives this as a tendency. The number of informants is not stated, and the study rests on one village.
S · Not every spirit of the house is an ancestor

S / 03 Not every spirit of the house is an ancestor The same article that calls the domovoy an ancestor sorts other household spirits differently. It places the bannik and his female counterpart, the obderikha, in a separate group as the most dangerous and malicious, and it traces the kikimora not to ancestors but to unbaptised dead infants. So the plate does not offer one class of ‘house spirit’. Even for the domovoy the ancestor reading is one scholar’s argument, repeated by others and kept by some informants; the 2015 urban survey did not find it, and Granova offers it as a possibility in the names. The atlas keeps it as a contested reading, not as the explanation.

T · A name made by a scholar

T / 01 A name made by a scholar ‘Zalozhnye pokoiniki’ is a scholar’s term. Dmitry Zelenin brought it into use in 1916, taking it from the dialect of Vyatka, where it meant dead who were ‘covered over’ with brushwood, boards or stakes instead of being laid in the earth. He understood it to reflect a belief that the earth does not receive such dead, and he used it for all the ‘impure’ dead. V. E. Ovseichik, working on the Belarusian-Russian borderland, declines to extend the word to the whole category: it does not occur in Belarusian or other traditions, and burial methods varied. The plate therefore uses ‘unquiet dead’ and ‘impure dead’ for the category and keeps ‘zalozhnye’ for what Zelenin meant by it.
T · Three categories in one borderland

T / 02 Three categories in one borderland Ovseichik’s material, from the Vitebsk, Pskov and Smolensk regions, centres on three groups. Unbaptised children were thought unable to enter paradise and to fly at night asking to be baptised; a symbolic baptism or naming after death is widespread. They were kept out of common cemeteries, a ban the author calls strictly enforced in the first half of the twentieth century. Later records mostly call such children angels. Suicides, in the same material, were thought to go to the devil, not to the ancestors. In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries the body was often not washed, was buried in the clothes it died in, with no funeral meal and no church service, and sometimes marked with an aspen stake. Reported burial places include crossroads, swamps, a ditch by the cemetery, hills and forest. Respondents expected drought and storms if a suicide lay in the common cemetery. Sorcerers were ‘impure’ whatever the manner of death, because the devil was thought to take the soul. They were buried outside the cemetery or by its fence. Radical measures are reported: exhuming the body, cutting off the head and setting it between the legs, driving an aspen stake through the body. The author cites one modern informant for this.
T · Walking dead and literary vampires

T / 03 Walking dead and literary vampires Ovseichik reports that sorcerers were believed to walk after death, harming people and drinking their blood, and adds that this is rare in the East Slavic area and more typical of South Slavic vampire lore. The borderland material is mostly about where and how the impure dead were buried, not about what they did once they rose. The upyr’ of nineteenth-century Russian fiction is another matter. One thesis abstract places the literary vampire as a device used in Russian writing from the eighteenth century on, built on older belief. The atlas keeps the two apart: the field records read for this plate do not describe a figure like the literary vampire, and nothing here is evidence for one.
T · A dispute about where the rule came from

T / 04 A dispute about where the rule came from Ethnographers of the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries took such burial customs for pagan survivals. A. Avdeev argues the opposite for Muscovite Russia: from sixteenth to early eighteenth-century epitaphs and letters of church hierarchs he finds no obstacle to cemetery burial or regular commemoration of those who died violent deaths, and he holds that the related superstitions arose in Christian times. This plate has the abstract only. It cannot say how strong Avdeev’s evidence is or how far his conclusion reaches beyond the Muscovite sources. It is placed here so that the pagan-survival reading is not left standing alone.

T / 05 A rule remembered, 2018–2019 A. Ryko’s fieldwork in the Khislavichi district of the Smolensk region found only remnants of such beliefs. Informants born in the 1930s remember that those who hanged or drowned themselves were not taken to the common cemetery; younger people say they know nothing of it and that the drowned lay in the cemetery. Unbaptised infants were not counted as ‘unclean’ there. No one now says that certain dead can return and harm the living. Set beside Ovseichik, the two studies cover neighbouring districts and different decades of the same century, and they do not agree on unbaptised children. The author says the findings rest on memory and that it is not clear whether the trend is local.

U / 01 The Church’s own list In a church instructional text, Hieromonk Job (Gumerov) names the Saturdays on which the Church commemorates the dead: Meat Fare Saturday, the second, third and fourth Saturdays of Great Lent, Trinity Saturday and St. Demetrius Saturday. He explains the choice of Saturday by its place as the day of rest, and says the Lenten Saturdays stand in for the daily memorial services that are suspended during the fast. He gives St. Demetrius Saturday a precise origin: it was set up after the battle of Kulikovo in 1380, with the blessing of Sergius of Radonezh, first for the soldiers who fell and later for all the departed. This is the Church’s account of itself, written by a churchman; it is evidence for what the Church holds, not for what a village did.
U · A day the church calendar does not have

U / 02 A day the church calendar does not have G. I. Maltsev records the commemoration days of the Komi-Permyaks: Radonitsa, Semik, Trinity Saturday, and the Saturdays before Pokrov and St. Demetrius. He writes that Semik, the Thursday of the seventh week after Easter, is absent from the Orthodox calendar, that priests took no part in it in the late nineteenth century and did from the early twentieth. After Zelenin he reports that those dead by unnatural death were commemorated at Semik, and quotes a Kungur saying that they are deaf and blind except on that day. He also describes a slow move: the Permyaks began to hold this commemoration on the Saturdays of general remembrance, reasoning that prayers would be heard better then. His material is four recordings by one researcher, from a people who are not Russian. The plate uses it only as a regional comparison for a pattern that Russian sources describe.

U / 03 A cemetery day, 2016–2017 E. G. Chesnokova’s fieldwork in the Kostroma and Vladimir regions found the main cemetery commemoration falling in either the Easter or the Trinity period, and she says this follows regional zones. Within the period one day carries the main rites, and she divides it into a preparation, a meeting of relatives at the cemetery, a walk among the graves, commemoration at the grave, and a continuation at home. She finds these days both family occasions and social ones, with their importance held or growing, and says collective commemoration repairs ties weakened by distance and broken family traditions. V · Two aims, and the acts that serve them

V / 01 Two aims, and the acts that serve them An encyclopedia article on East Slavic funeral rites says the rite works in two directions: some acts help the dead reach the other world, others protect the living from the dead. Its protective and cleansing acts include washing the house after the coffin is carried out, turning objects over, covering mirrors and washing hands on returning from the cemetery. Its prohibitions include close relatives making the coffin and bringing food back from the cemetery. The explanation the article gives is general: the dead can harm the living, and the boundary between worlds stays open from the death until the burial and the fortieth day. It does not give a reason for each separate act, and it does not date its examples. The page does not name an author.

V / 02 In the house J. Rouhier-Willoughby, in a review of urban funerals, lists what the older village rite is reported to have included: candles lit, all the mirrors in the house covered, all water thrown out. She says mirrors were thought symbolically close to water, which is why both were treated the same. The women who washed the body turned tables and benches over before washing them, she writes, so that death would enter the soil; a priest might also say a prayer of purification once the body had been carried out. She draws these from earlier ethnographers, so the village custom reaches the atlas at second hand. For the urban twentieth century she reports that the covering of shiny surfaces continued.

V / 03 Washing Washing the body appears in both sources as an obligatory part of the rite. The encyclopedia cites a scholar who argues that the strictness of the rule points to a purpose beyond cleaning: removing what marked the person as living. In the Russian North, it says, older women past childbearing were often hired to wash the dead. In the Khislavichi district of Smolensk, A. Ryko’s informants said neighbours were invited to wash, women washing women and men washing men, and she found no stated ban on relatives taking part. Where the encyclopedia lists a prohibition, her district does not report it. The two sources describe different places and cannot be added together.

V / 04 Done without an explanation Ryko writes that people in the borderland often perform funeral actions without being able to say what they are for, and that as the motives fade the sense of obligation fades with them. This is her observation of one district, based on informants’ memories, and she says it is unclear whether the trend is local. It matters here because the reasons attached to protective acts in the other sources are the reasons collected from or ascribed to people at particular times. They are not a fixed meaning that every act always carried.

V / 05 Why the mirror? Several reasons are on record for covering mirrors. A hieromonk, writing against the custom, reports that people said the soul should not be frightened by its reflection, or the dead should not frighten the family, or the soul might pass into the mirror. Rouhier-Willoughby, reporting scholarship, ties mirrors to water, which was also thrown out. These do not agree with each other and none is shown here to be the original. The church writer is hostile and gives the folk reasons in order to dismiss them. The atlas lists the reasons and leaves the meaning of the act unsettled.

V / 06 The Church’s position Hieromonk Dometian calls the covering of mirrors a folk custom with nothing in common with the Orthodox burial rite, and he says the same of overturning tables and chairs, which he calls pagan survivals. He also reports a belief that one must not look out of a window at a funeral procession, and he tells believers to take the blessing of a priest as their only guide. This is a polemical text of unstated date. It shows what the Church objects to, and by implication what was practised, but it is not a count of practice.

W / 01 Novosibirsk: dated decisions, as reported In a 2023 interview, E. Krasilnikova of Novosibirsk State Technical University dates a run of local decisions. A 1920 decision concerned cutting the grove at the cemetery. In 1929 the Voskresenskaya church was ordered closed, and in April 1930 a crowd of about a thousand protested and was dispersed by the militia. The old cemetery became a garden and later part of a park; the church went to the park administration, held a planetarium and burned in the 1970s. She places the start of such demolitions in Siberia in the mid-1920s. The interview states the dates as facts but cites no file or archive for them, so they stand here as the interviewee’s report.

W / 02 Barnaul and Omsk In her account two large cemeteries in Barnaul were destroyed in the 1930s, graves were opened for valuables and remains left scattered. She calls Barnaul the most radical case in Siberia; that comparison is her judgement. Omsk went another way. She says its historic necropolis survived until the 1950s, was recorded and photographed by a museum director before its demolition, and in 2005 fragments of its stones were gathered into a memorial square. Novosibirsk has no comparable memorial, she adds.

X · A dissertation on mourning online

X / 02 A dissertation on mourning online K. Linden’s doctoral dissertation at Uppsala studies online commemoration in the Russian-speaking world by virtual ethnography of three memorial sites, among them one on Soviet repressions and one on the Nord-Ost siege, together with social networking sites. She argues that online tools enable communal remembrance, that this has three sides (between the living and the dead, among mourners, and as motive for action), and that digitalisation may challenge a political culture of forgetting. She also argues that the ‘right to be forgotten’ is not necessarily the answer, because difficulty in forgetting online could help repair a broken memory culture. This is an argument within her theoretical framework. The atlas has the library abstract only and treats it as her claim.

They describe AI avatars of the dead, which can recreate voice and habits and can also produce errors, with a comparison to Frankenstein’s creature. The two effects are put forward together by the researchers themselves, and the atlas leaves both open. The plate has a university news item, not the article. The item does not discuss Russian law.

1380 · St. Demetrius Saturday is set up

After the battle of Kulikovo a Saturday of commemoration is instituted, first for the fallen soldiers and later for all the departed, with the blessing of Sergius of Radonezh. This is the Church’s own account of the origin, as a churchman tells it.

The Last Judgment icon from the Nativity monastery in Novgorod is painted in registers, with the saved and the damned arranged as populations. It is an image made to be read, and it will remain the basic model for Russian judgement pictures for centuries.
10 October 1723 · Peter I restricts burial inside towns

A decree orders that the overcrowded churchyard cemeteries be moved outside the city, with an exception for ‘notable persons’, and orders raised tombs levelled. After Peter’s death the churchyard burial resumes; the measure is a precedent more than a settlement.

Tens of thousands die. Grigorii Orlov is sent to Moscow with emergency powers; the dead are buried outside the city, and the new cemetery at Vagankovo begins with unnamed plague victims. Mass death produces the modern out-of-town cemetery.
1771 · Burial in communal pits is banned

The online encyclopedia entry on Semik says that unidentified and unclaimed bodies were once placed in open communal pits, skudelnitsy, and that Catherine II banned burial in them in 1771. The entry is anonymous and cites no decree.
An icon of the Last Judgment is painted in the Volga region, 180 × 137 cm. Its compartments and inscribed bands derive from printed engravings: the judgement has become a page.

Archbishop Veniamin’s handbook sets out the rationale for commemoration on the third, ninth and fortieth days: the Resurrection, the nine ranks of angels, the Ascension. It is the clearest statement of the scheme that later writers would call a folk custom.
The collection of Russian folktales on which a 2025 reading of Baba-Yaga’s hut as a threshold rests. The folktales are narrative, not a record of burial practice.
1865 · Perov paints Seeing Off the Dead

A small canvas, 45.3 × 57 cm, of a family carrying a coffin on a sled. The painting becomes a reference point for the representation of peasant death and is later connected by the gallery to Nekrasov’s poem of 1862–63.

Three volumes of funeral laments recorded in the Olonets region establish lament as a composed, performed genre with named performers and a repertoire. This is the moment the Russian lament becomes an archive.

An unknown photographer records a memorial meal at Smolensk cemetery in St Petersburg. It is one of the few nineteenth-century photographs in this atlas that shows the ritual meal rather than the monument.
Tolstoy’s novella turns the deathbed into a corridor. It is not an ethnographic document; it is evidence of how the educated Russian reader was invited to imagine dying.

D. K. Zelenin publishes his study of those who die an unnatural death and of the rusalki, and gives the category zalozhnye pokoiniki its lasting form. The book is a synthesis, and its category is an argument.

Revolution and civil war break the institutions that had produced most of the sources above: parishes, monasteries, consistories, the ethnographic collections of the imperial academies. After this point, the atlas’s sources change kind.
1925 · Moscow Soviet decides to build a crematorium
The decision chooses the church of St Seraphim of Sarov and St Anna of Kashin at the Donskoy Monastery as the site. The first cremation follows in 1927.

A crematorium opens in the church of St Seraphim of Sarov and St Anna of Kashin at the Donskoy Monastery. The first cremation takes place on 12 January; the official opening follows on 6 October 1927, without ceremony.
1920–1930 · Novosibirsk: cemetery grove, church closure, protest

In the account of E. Krasilnikova, a 1920 decision concerned cutting the grove at the cemetery, the Voskresenskaya church was ordered closed in 1929, and in April 1930 a crowd of about a thousand protested and was dispersed by the militia. The old cemetery became a garden and later part of a park.

The destruction or truncation of monastic and parish burial grounds in the Soviet period is well attested in general terms, but it has not been itemised by this atlas. The record here is a gap, not a list.

In Krasilnikova’s account two large cemeteries in Barnaul were destroyed in the 1930s, graves were opened for valuables and remains left scattered. She calls Barnaul the most radical case in Siberia; that comparison is her judgement.
1935 · Malevich buried under a black square
The painter is buried near Nemchinovka. A white cube with a black square marks the grave. The oak is cut down, the grave is lost, and the cube disappears.
1 August 1936 · Decree on resettlement from the flood zone

An article on Cherepovets district states that resettlement followed a decree of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee and the Council of People’s Commissars of that date, and that the residents of about seven hundred villages and hamlets were moved out of the flood zone. The decree itself was not seen.
Hundreds of thousands die in Leningrad and are buried in mass graves that become the ground of the Piskaryovskoye memorial. The sites are administrative before they are sacred.
The ensemble by A. V. Vasil’ev and E. A. Levinson opens on the fifteenth anniversary of victory. The flame is carried from the Field of Mars, where it had been lit in 1957.
8 May 1967 · The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

The monument by Dmitrii Burdin, Vladimir Klimov and Iurii Rabaev, with the sculptor Nikolai Tomskii, opens at the Kremlin wall. An unmanageable number of war dead is converted into one body that can be visited.

The state monopoly on funeral services ends; commercial funeral homes, municipal fee schedules and, later, online memorials appear. Orthodoxy returns to public ritual. The atlas marks this period as under-researched rather than describing it as a unified new culture of death.
2005 · Omsk gathers fragments of its necropolis into a square

Krasilnikova says the historic necropolis of Omsk survived until the 1950s and was recorded and photographed by a museum director before its demolition. In 2005 fragments of its stones were gathered into a memorial square. Novosibirsk has no comparable memorial.
2010 · The census counts villages with no inhabitants

Press reports of the 2010 census figures put the number of villages that exist de jure but have no inhabitants at 19,400, up from 13,000, and say 36,200 villages have fewer than ten residents. The reports give figures, not the fate of the cemeteries.
2013–2021 · Roadside memorial signs counted on three highways

M. G. Matlin drives sections of three federal highways in the Middle Volga repeatedly and documents 299 roadside memorial signs, with dates of death from 1965 to 2019. He sorts them into a family that imitates the cemetery and one that does not.
2016–2017 · Fieldwork on cemetery commemoration in Kostroma and Vladimir
E. G. Chesnokova’s fieldwork finds the main cemetery commemoration falling in the Easter or the Trinity period, following regional zones. Only the abstract was read.
2018–2019 · Fieldwork in Khislavichi district, Smolensk region

A. Ryko records that informants born in the 1930s remember a ban on taking those who hanged or drowned themselves to the common cemetery, while younger people say they know nothing of it. Neighbours washed the dead, women washing women and men washing men. She says the findings rest on memory and that it is unclear whether the trend is local.
June 2019 · Domovoy beliefs recorded in Severny Kommunar

M. A. Granova records beliefs about the domovoy in Severny Kommunar, Sivinsky district, Perm Krai, and compares them with older university-archive material. She finds the beliefs much reduced and gives this as a tendency; the number of informants is not stated.
2019 · Gravestones found used as curbs on Bersenevskaya Embankment

A municipal deputy posts photographs of gravestones used as curbs near the Estrada Theatre in Moscow; some stones still show dates of birth and death. The construction department says the work was not under its direction. The find is known through the photographs and an outlet’s report, not through an inspection record.
2020 · A study of the digital afterlife of Russian internet users

A. Sergeeva, R. Gerlit and H. Krcmar analyse 33 social networks and online services, survey 173 users and interview experts. Their abstract expects services to host more deceased than living users in the coming decades. This is a projection; only the abstract was read.
2023 · Muon survey in the Pskov-Caves Monastery

A team lays nuclear-emulsion detectors in the caves at Pechory to image two objects with atmospheric muons. The newspaper account reports a hidden passage of about 12 m behind a walled crypt, a continuation of Trinity Street and a cavity of roughly 3 × 6 × 3 m. These are the team’s estimates as quoted, not checked by opening.

The container in which the body is carried and buried. Described in the ethnography as plain, made of planks, sometimes hollowed from a single trunk in northern accounts. By the late imperial period it is increasingly a purchased object. It appears in plate B as furniture, in plate C as the centre of the rite, and in plate J as the box that organises Perov’s painting.

The cross set on the grave; several formal types are recorded. Eight-pointed, six-pointed and four-pointed crosses are all found on Russian graves, with regional and period variation. The roofed cross (golubets) shelters the cross under a gable and turns the grave into a small building. The atlas draws four types as measured elevations and marks the drawings as reconstructions.

Lit at the funeral, at memorial services and at the grave. A small, expendable object with a long life in the sources: it marks the presence of prayer, it is placed in the hand or beside the body in some descriptions, and it is bought and carried by mourners. The atlas uses it as a graphic sign for the presence of ritual time.

The stone, cross or structure that identifies a grave. In the medieval and early modern period the marker might be a stone slab or a wooden cross; from the eighteenth century the monument becomes an architectural object with an inscription, a portrait or a symbol. The atlas keeps the marker and the grave separate: a grave can exist without a marker, and a marker can survive its grave.

Cloth that covers or wraps the body. Regionally variable in form and name: a shroud, a covering, a piece of linen. Its function is to separate the body from the hands that carry it and to present the dead as a figure rather than a corpse. The atlas does not illustrate a specific example because it has not verified one.

Bread, pancakes or grain preparations eaten at the memorial meal. Bread and bliny recur in descriptions of the memorial table; the grain dish kutya is the most explicitly ritual of the foods. The atlas treats the food as an object with a documented context and an undocumented prehistory.

Boiled grain sweetened with honey, eaten at memorial meals and blessed at memorial services. Wheat or rice, honey, later raisins. The church dish is called kolivo; household kutya may be richer. The grain is read as a figure of resurrection. The relationship between the two dishes is not settled by the sources used here.

The bowl, cup or dish reserved for the memorial meal or for the dead. A place is set for the dead in some accounts, with a cup or a portion. The object is unremarkable in itself; what makes it ritual is the reservation — it is not used for the living.

The formal entrance to a cemetery, with a wall and often a chapel. From the late eighteenth century the cemetery is a walled, gated, planned space. The gate is the point at which the funeral procession changes register: from street to enclosure. The atlas draws a schematic plan rather than a survey.

The image that survives when the grave does not. Photographs are the atlas’s main evidence for cemeteries and memorials, and also its main source of error: a photograph documents a moment of maintenance, not a state. The portrait on a headstone is a different object again, and one the atlas has not been able to document.

A painted image of a holy figure or feast, used in worship and in the funeral rite. The Last Judgment icon is the atlas’s central image of the afterlife: a diagram of judgement with inscribed compartments. The Dormition icon supplies the model of the good death. Both are shown as historical objects, not as illustrations of doctrine.

Covered in the house after a death in many recorded accounts. The practice is widely reported; the explanation is not stable, and the atlas marks the chronology of the custom as unknown. It is included in the object index because it is the most frequently cited material sign of the threshold.

The low metal or wooden fence around a plot. A ubiquitous feature of Russian cemeteries in the twentieth century, and almost entirely absent from the sources used here. The atlas notes it as an object that everyone has seen and no one has documented.

A state-built ensemble commemorating collective death. From the late 1950s the Soviet state built large ensembles — Piskaryovskoye, Mamayev Kurgan, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier — that combined architecture, sculpture, landscape and ceremony. They are documents of how the state wanted the dead to be seen.

A continuously burning flame at a memorial. The flame on the Field of Mars in Leningrad was lit in 1957; the flame at Piskaryovskoye was lit from it at the memorial’s opening in 1960. The flame is a technology of memory: it requires maintenance, and its maintenance is the state’s promise.

The border between the living and the dead, maintained by prohibitions rather than by a wall. Used for the set of small adjustments made around a death: the opened window, the covered mirror, the water thrown out, the body carried out. The term is analytical; the sources describe the practices, not the concept.

The part of the person that survives death; described in both theological and folk registers. Orthodox doctrine and folk belief use the same word (dusha) for different constructions: a created immortal substance judged by God, and a breath-like presence that lingers near the body and must be fed and escorted. The atlas keeps the registers apart.

The dead coming back, or being treated as if they might. The returning dead are a way of talking about unfinished obligation. The atlas distinguishes the ethnographic reports (documented) from the category built on them (interpretation).

The washing of the body and the separation of the living from the dead. Washing is both practical and symbolic. The atlas treats it as a technique for handling the dead at arm’s length, and avoids claims about its pre-Christian origin.

The social and emotional work of loss, performed in public or withheld. In the Russian twentieth century mourning was repeatedly reorganised: by the Church, by the Soviet state and by the family. The atlas follows the distinction between public commemoration and private grief.

The scheduled repetition of prayer, food and naming. Remembrance in this atlas is a calendar and a set of objects: days three, nine and forty, the annual commemoration, the meal, the name spoken aloud. It is the most documented form of relation with the dead.

The use of the dead by the living — personal, familial, national. Memory is treated here as a practice with owners and budgets. The state’s memory is built at memorial complexes; the family’s memory at the table and at the grave.

The state of a grave, a cemetery or a name that no one maintains. Abandonment is what memory turns into when nobody tends it. The atlas documents it as a condition of the material record, and marks its own inability to survey it.

The imagined geography of the dead. The atlas distinguishes the doctrinal claim (judgement, resurrection, communion with God) from the iconographic and folk geography (scales, rivers of fire, roads, places of waiting).
